newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Miners see few answers in Australian PM title plan.
newsitem.headline: Miners see few answers in Australian PM title plan.

text.p: The Minerals Council of Australia said on Wednesday Prime Minister John Howard's ten-point plan on Native Title provided few answers.
Access to land for exploration and development on certain and reasonable terms was essential for the minerals industry's future in Australia, executive director Dick Wells said in a statement.
The Minerals Council had concerns after a preliminary assessment of the plan, he said.
The potential existed for a state regime to cover leasehold land and a Federal regime to cover Crown (state) land, he said.
"The final plan must provide a long-term solution that is durable and delivers certainty if it is to be judged a success," he said.

Prime Minister Howard has not publicly released full details of his ten-point plan but main provisions covering mining on vacant Crown land call for a higher registration test for Aboriginal claimants seeking the right to negotiate.
The plan calls for no negotiations on exploration, and only one right to negotiate per project.

For mining on other non-exclusive tenures, such as current or former pastoral leasehold land and national parks, the right to negotiate would continue to apply in a state or territory in the absence of a statutory regime acceptable to the Federal government.

Howard has been attempting to resolve a major dispute between Aboriginals and Australian farmers and miners which followed a High Court decision of last December which ruled in a case involving the Wik tribe that pastoral leases and native title could co-exist.
Farmers have been pressing for full extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases but have said Howard's ten-point plan indicates some progress in the dispute.
The Minerals Council statement on Wednesday breaks the mining industry's recent silence on the issue.
Negotiations between mining groups and Aboriginals over native title claims over new mine proposals on Crown land or land covered by pastoral leases have unsettled or slowed new mine proposals.
